source_text: Nunc ut simplicius respondeamus, non competebat ex semine humano dei filium nasci, 'ne, si totus esset filius hominis, non esset et dei filius, nihilque haberet amplios Salomone, et amplius Iona; aut de Hebionis opinione credendus erat. Ergo iam dei Ã­llius ex patris dei semine, id est spiritu, ut esset et hominis illius, caro ei sola competebat ex hominis carne sumenda sine viri semine. Vacabat enim semen viri apud habentem dei semen. Itaque sicut nondum natus ex virgine patrem deum habere potuit sine homine matre, aeque cum de virgime nasceretur, potuit matrem habere hominem sine homine patre. Sic denique homo cum deo, dum caro hominis cum spiritu dei; caro sine semine ex homine, spiritus cum semine ex deo. Igitur si fuit dispositio rationis super filium dei ex virgine proferendum, cur non ex virgine acceperit corpus, quod de virgine protulit? Quia aliud est quod a deo sumpsit, quoniam, inquiunt, verbum caro factum est. Vox ista quid caro factum sit coutestatur, nec tamen periclitatur quasi statim aliud sit factum caro, et non verbum. Si ex carne factum est verbum caro, aut si ex "semine ipso factum est, "scriptura dicat. Cum scriptura non "dicat nisi quod sit factum, non et unde sit factum, ergo ex alio, non ex semetipso suggerit factum. Si non ex semetipso, sed ex alio, iam hinc tracta ex quo magis credere congruat carnem factum verbum, nisi ex carne, in qua et factum est, vel quia ipse dominus sententialiter et definitive pronuntiavit, Quod in carne natum est, caro est, quia ex carne natum est. Sed si de homine tantummodo dixit, non et de semetipso, plane nega hominem Christum, et ila defende non et in ipsum competisse. Atquin subicit: Et quod de spiritu natum est, spiritus est, quia deus spiritus est, et de deo natus est. Hoc utique vel eo magis in ipsum tendit, si et in credentes eius. Si ergo et hoc ad ipsum, cur non et illud supra? Neque enim dividere potes hoc ad ipsum, illud supra ad ceteros homines, qui utramque substantiam Christi et carnis et spiritus non negas. Ceterum si tam carnem habuit quam spiritum, cum de duarum substantiarum conditione pronuntiat quas et ipse gestat, non potest videri de spiritu quidem suo, de carne vero non sua determinasse. Ita cum ipse sit de spiritu dei et spirtus deus est, ex deo natus ipse est et ex carne hominis, homo in carne generatus.
thought_title: Why the Son of God took flesh without human seed
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that Christ should not have been born of a virgin, by explaining why he took flesh from Mary without a human father.
pass_a_gloss: Now, so that we may answer more simply, it was not fitting for the Son of God to be born from human seed, lest, if he were wholly Son of Man, he would not also be Son of God, and would have nothing more than Solomon, and more than Jonah; or he would have to be believed according to the opinion of Ebion. Therefore, since he was already the Son of God from the seed of God the Father, that is, the Spirit, so that he might also be Son of Man, flesh alone was fitting for him, to be taken from the flesh of man without the seed of a man. For the seed of a man was idle in one who had the seed of God. And so, just as, not yet born from the virgin, he was able to have God as father without a human mother, equally, when he was born from the virgin, he was able to have a human mother without a human father. Thus, finally, man with God, while flesh of man with Spirit of God; flesh without seed from man, Spirit with seed from God. Therefore, if there was a plan of reason for the Son of God to be brought forth from a virgin, why would he not have received from the virgin the body which he brought forth from the virgin? Because it is one thing which he took from God, since, they say, the Word was made flesh. This utterance testifies what was made flesh, and yet it is not endangered as if something other than the Word was immediately made flesh, and not the Word. If the Word was made flesh from flesh, or if it was made from seed itself, let Scripture say so. Since Scripture does not say except that it was made, not also from what it was made, therefore it suggests that it was made from another, not from itself. If not from itself, but from another, now from this point consider from what it is more fitting to believe the Word was made flesh, except from the flesh in which it was also made, or because the Lord himself pronounced as a sentence and definitively, What is born in the flesh is flesh, because it is born from flesh. But if he said this only about man, and not also about himself, plainly deny that Christ is man, and so defend that it did not also apply to him. But he adds: And what is born of the Spirit is spirit, because God is Spirit, and he is born of God. This certainly tends toward him all the more, if also toward those who believe in him. If therefore this also applies to him, why not also the former? For you cannot divide this as applying to him, and the former as applying to other men, you who do not deny both substances of Christ, of flesh and of spirit. Otherwise, if he had flesh as much as spirit, when he pronounces about the condition of the two substances which he himself also bears, he cannot be seen to have determined about his own spirit indeed, but not about his own flesh. Thus, since he himself is of the Spirit of God and the Spirit is God, he himself is born of God, and from the flesh of man, man generated in flesh.

pass_b_english: Now, to answer more simply: it was not fitting for the Son of God to be born from human seed, because if he were entirely Son of Man, he would not also be Son of God, and he would have nothing more than Solomon or Jonah. In that case, he would have to be believed according to Ebion's opinion. Therefore, since he was already the Son of God from the seed of God the Father—that is, the Spirit—the only flesh that suited him, so that he might also be Son of Man, was flesh taken from the flesh of man without a man's seed. A man's seed had no role for one who already had God's seed.

Just as he could have God as Father without a human mother before he was born of the virgin, so when he was born of the virgin he could have a human mother without a human father. In this way he is man with God, since his flesh is the flesh of man with the Spirit of God: flesh without seed from a human being, Spirit with seed from God. If it was the plan of reason that the Son of God should be brought forth from a virgin, why would he not receive from the virgin the body he brought forth from the virgin? Because what he took from God is one thing, they say, since the Word was made flesh (John 1:14).

This phrase testifies what was made flesh, but it is not endangered as if something other than the Word was suddenly made flesh. If the Word was made flesh out of flesh, or if it was made out of seed itself, let Scripture say so. Since Scripture says only what was made, not also from what it was made, it suggests that it was made from something else, not from itself. If not from itself but from something else, then consider from what it is more fitting to believe the Word was made flesh—if not from the flesh in which it was also made. The Lord himself pronounced this as a settled and definitive judgment: What is born of the flesh is flesh (John 3:6), because it is born of flesh.

But if he said this only about man and not about himself, then plainly deny that Christ is man, and in that way defend that it did not apply to him. Yet he adds: And what is born of the Spirit is Spirit (John 3:6)—because God is Spirit (John 4:24), and he is born of God. This certainly points to him all the more, if it also points to those who believe in him. If this applies to him, why not the earlier statement too? You cannot divide it so that this applies to him and the earlier statement applies to other men—not if you do not deny both substances of Christ, flesh and Spirit. Since he had both flesh and Spirit, when he pronounces on the condition of the two substances which he himself bears, he cannot be seen to have determined about his Spirit but not about his flesh. So since he himself is of the Spirit of God and the Spirit is God, he is born of God; and he is of the flesh of man, a man generated in flesh.

problems.quote: because God is Spirit, and he is born of God (John 3:6)
problems.source_quote: quia deus spiritus est, et de deo natus est
problems.why: John 3:6 stops at is spirit. God is Spirit is John 4:24; the rest is Tertullian's gloss.
problems.fix: is Spirit (John 3:6)—because God is Spirit (John 4:24), and he is born of God.
problems.ruling: 'quia deus spiritus est, et de deo natus est' is Tertullian's gloss, not John 3:6; the citation tag misattributes it to Scripture.

problems.quote: because it is born of flesh (John 3:6)
problems.source_quote: caro est, quia ex carne natum est
problems.why: John 3:6 does not give this because-clause; it is Tertullian's own explanation.
problems.fix: is flesh (John 3:6), because it is born from flesh.
problems.ruling: 'quia ex carne natum est' is Tertullian's explanation, not in John 3:6; the reference wrongly attaches to the because-clause.

problems.quote: In that case, we would have to believe the opinion of Ebion.
problems.source_quote: aut de Hebionis opinione credendus erat
problems.why: The subject of 'credendus erat' is the Son of God: he would have to be believed (to be a mere man) on Ebion's opinion. English makes 'we' believe Ebion's opinion.
problems.fix: Otherwise he would have to be believed on Ebion's opinion (a mere man).
problems.ruling: credendus erat is passive: the Son must be believed de Hebionis opinione, not that we believe Ebion’s opinion.

fixed: wrong_scripture flesh clause: source 'caro est, quia ex carne natum est' — John 3:6 ends at 'is flesh', quia-clause is Tertullian's gloss, so citation moved inside.
wrong_scripture Spirit clause: source 'quia deus spiritus est, et de deo natus est' — John 3:6 ends at 'is Spirit'; 'God is Spirit' is John 4:24 and remainder is gloss, so citations split.
agency Ebion: source 'aut de Hebionis opinione credendus erat' has Son of God as subject of credendus erat, so changed 'we believe' to 'he would have to be believed'.

last_rejected.quote: he cannot be seen to have determined about his Spirit but not about his flesh
last_rejected.source_quote: non potest videri de spiritu quidem suo, de carne vero non sua determinasse
last_rejected.why: Non modifies sua: he did not define his own Spirit on one side and flesh that was not his own on the other.
last_rejected.fix: he cannot be seen to have defined his own Spirit on the one hand and flesh that was not his own on the other.
last_rejected.ruling: "de carne vero non sua" is rendered "about his flesh"; the 'not his own' nuance is lost, but the argument that he spoke of both his substances survives.

last_rejected.quote: What is born of the flesh is flesh (John 3:6), because it is born of flesh.
last_rejected.source_quote: Quod in carne natum est, caro est, quia ex carne natum est.
last_rejected.why: In carne means born in the flesh; ex carne is a separate claim, born from flesh.
last_rejected.fix: What is born in the flesh is flesh, because it is born of flesh.
last_rejected.ruling: "in carne natum" as "born of the flesh" is the normal John 3:6 wording. It is within the range of meaning and does not mislead the argument.

last_rejected.quote: This phrase testifies what was made flesh, but it is not endangered as if something other than the Word was suddenly made flesh.
last_rejected.source_quote: Vox ista quid caro factum sit coutestatur, nec tamen periclitatur quasi statim aliud sit factum caro, et non verbum.
last_rejected.why: Meaning: the phrase attests what became flesh (the Word), and there is no risk that something else, not the Word, became flesh. English is garbled and vague about 'suddenly'/'statim'.
last_rejected.fix: This phrase attests what became flesh, and there is no danger that something else became flesh at once, and not the Word.
last_rejected.ruling: Vox...contestatur plus nec periclitatur quasi...aliud...non verbum is kept; statim as 'suddenly' is loose, not a meaning reversal.

last_rejected.quote: if not from the flesh in which it was also made
last_rejected.source_quote: ex quo magis credere congruat carnem factum verbum, nisi ex carne, in qua et factum est
last_rejected.why: 'nisi' means 'than/except': from what is it more fitting to believe the Word became flesh, if not from flesh? English 'if not' garbles the argument and 'in which' is ambiguous.
last_rejected.fix: from what is it more fitting to believe the Word became flesh than from the flesh in which it was made?
last_rejected.ruling: nisi ex carne is already 'if not from the flesh'; in qua et factum est matches 'in which it was also made.'
